entries.title: Englewood dad fatally shot in his home was family's 'protector,' fiancé says
entries.summary: <p>Jennifer Lacey felt like 2026 was going to be her year. </p><p>She had just gotten promoted at work. Her kids were doing well. And she had just moved into a new home with her fiancé, Antwan Washington.</p><p>Then her 11-year-old son woke up to find bullet holes in the living room wall and his dad motionless on the couch. At first, Lacey thought he was asleep.</p><p>"From the position he was sitting, it looked like he was asleep," Lacey said. "So I tapped him, like, 'Babe, get up. You have to get to work.' ... He just falls to the right, and that's when I see that he was shot in the head. ... Just the worst day of my life, ever."</p><p>Washington, 45, had been shot in the head and was pronounced dead on the scene, according to Chicago police.</p><p>He was in his home watching TV in the 5700 block of South May Street around 5 a.m. Saturday when two people got out of a gray 4-door sedan and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/28/man-fatally-shot-inside-englewood-home" >fired handguns into the apartment</a>, according to a police report. The car fled the scene. Police found 16 shell casings in the intersection.</p><p>"He wasn't doing anything but doing his normal morning routine: getting up in the morning, you know, washing up, brushing his teeth, you know, getting dressed and making his coffee and smoking his cigarette," Lacey, 33, said through tears.</p><p>The police report states that someone else in the building was the intended target of the shooting.</p><p>"There's really no motivation for it," Lacey said. "We're just a working family just wanting to raise our kids." </p><p>Now Lacey is grappling with the aftermath of his death. She must now raise their four sons without their father. Her future plans are shattered: a housewarming party at their new home, hosting family for barbecues and watching their kids grow up. Washington also leaves behind a 21-year-old son from a previous relationship, she said.</p><p>"I will continue to let my kids know how much he did love them, how much of a leader he was, and how much positivity he instilled in them as children," she said.</p><p>Lacey described Washington as a "protector" who worked hard and loved his family. He could often be found playing video games with his sons, barbecuing in the summer and listening to Earth, Wind & Fire or 2Pac. He was a manager at an Englewood Chipotle and had recently moved to manage a team at a Bridgeport location, Lacey said.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/support-for-antwans-family-after-tragic-loss" target="_blank" >GoFundMe</a> set up by his fiancée had raised $2,500 of a $10,000 goal by Monday night. It said the "simple moments meant everything to him and his family."</p><p><i>Contributing: Violet Miller</i></p>

entries.title: Miguel Vargas’ grand slam helps White Sox shake off season-opening ‘jitters’ for first win
entries.summary: <p>MIAMI — Maybe they just needed a few extra days to warm up.</p><p>After only showing signs of life late in a disastrous opening weekend, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> hitters found their stride Monday against the Marlins, clubbing their way to a 9-4 victory for their first triumph of the season.</p><p>A monster six-RBI night from Miguel Vargas in humid Miami made the Sox’ season-opening misery in blustery Milwaukee feel hundreds of miles away, even if their pitching woes kept things more interesting than fans would like.</p><p>Everson Pereira warmed up the Sox in the third inning by lining a double down the left-field line. He later scored on a single by Vargas.</p><p>Munetaka Murakami didn’t extend his historic three-game home-run streak to start his MLB career, but he did notch his first hit to stay in the park on a dribbler down the third-base line that set the stage for a three-run homer by Austin Hays, his first blast since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/21/white-sox-outfielder-austin-hays-brings-steadying-force-to-lineup" target="_blank" ><u>signing with the Sox</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Stay fair. IT WILL ❗️ <a href="https://t.co/cMZwl8mN2D">pic.twitter.com/cMZwl8mN2D</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2038760220638224720?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>In the fourth, Marlins starter Chris Paddack hit Luisangel Acuna with a pitch to load the bases after singles by Tristan Peters and Pereira. Then Vargas, a native of Cuba who lives in Miami, launched one 402 feet into the left-field seats for the Sox’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/29/white-sox-colson-montgomery-grand-slam-murakami-homer" target="_blank" ><u>second grand slam in as many days</u></a>. He had dozens of supporters in attendance at loanDepot Park.</p><p>‘‘Especially to have my family here and a couple of friends that never watched me play in the big leagues, it’s super-fun, and I’m very proud to accomplish what we accomplished today,’’ Vargas said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">MIGUEL VARGAS GRAND SLAM<br><br>LET’S GOOOOOO <a href="https://t.co/gmGOmxMhG5">pic.twitter.com/gmGOmxMhG5</a></p>— Mike (@ChiSoxFanMike) <a href="https://twitter.com/ChiSoxFanMike/status/2038764128932676030?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But no lead feels particularly comfortable for Sox pitchers, and right-hander Davis Martin served up a two-run homer to Liam Hicks in the fourth. The Marlins struck again in the fifth with an RBI single by Jakob Marsee.</p><p>All told, Martin allowed three runs and five hits with six strikeouts and two walks in five innings.</p><p></p><p>The Sox added a run in the sixth when Acuna walked, stole second and third and then slid home on a shallow sacrifice fly by Vargas, his sixth RBI of the evening.</p><p></p><p>Offseason addition Sean Newcomb was strong in relief until a triple by Marsee and a single by Otto Lopez narrowed the Sox’ lead to 9-4 in the eighth. He left a bases-loaded jam for Jordan Hicks to shut down.</p><p></p><p>After thwacking a grand slam in a losing cause when the Sox’ bullpen melted down Sunday against the Brewers, Colson Montgomery said he and other Sox hitters finally were shaking off <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/28/colson-montgomery-white-sox-year-2" target="_blank" ><u>some early-season nerves</u></a>. After being outscored 20-3 in their first two games, the Sox have stacked up 16 runs in two days.</p><p></p><p>‘‘We all progressively just kept getting better,’’ said Montgomery, who needed 74 career games to sock his first two grand slams, the fastest in Sox history. ‘‘We are seeing the ball a lot better, having better-quality at-bats. I think it was the jitters and we were all really excited.’’</p><p></p><p>Pereira acknowledged as much before his second consecutive multihit game after flailing through three strikeouts on Opening Day.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I’m one of those players that is really excited, and I want to crush every single pitch,’’ Pereira said. ‘‘Just try to slow the game down and breathe.’’</p><p></p><p>Now the Sox are hoping the offensive results multiply.</p><p></p><p>‘‘It’s just part of the game,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘You spend all this time in spring training and going about your business, and then the lights come on and it means something and it changes a little bit. You’ve just got to find your bearings again.’’</p><p></p><p>Vargas found his bearings while borrowing Murakami’s first-baseman’s mitt.</p><p></p><p>‘‘He got three homers in three games, and now I use it and I got one,’’ Vargas said. ‘‘So I might be keeping it with me.’’</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.summary: <p>MIAMI — The first several games of the automated ball/strike era have been a mixed bag for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>.</p><p>Catcher <b>Edgar Quero</b> hasn’t been shy about questioning umpires under the new ABS challenge system implemented <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/02/12/how-abs-challenge-system-will-affect-mlb-tv-broadcasts-chicago-cubs-white-sox-spring-training-schedules" target="_blank" ><u>this season</u></a>, but Sox hitters still are feeling it out.</p><p>‘‘We’ve seen them less willing to pull the trigger on some challenges,’’ manager <b>Will Venable</b> said. ‘‘And I don’t get instant feedback on all these pitches on where they’re at, but it seems like we’re seeing less challenges from hitters.’’</p><p>Through four games, <b>Lenyn Sosa</b>, <b>Tristan Peters</b> and <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> are the only Sox batters to challenge calls. Sosa and Peters were wrong, but Murakami wiped out a miscalled strike Monday.</p><p>Quero has challenged nine calls behind the plate, getting four bad ones overturned. Sox pitchers have yet to initiate a review.</p><p>So should the Sox be quicker to tap their hat or helmet?</p><p>‘‘If they’re right, yeah,’’ Venable said with a laugh. ‘‘We want to make sure we’re challenging the right pitches. . . . It’s still new for a lot of these guys.’’</p><p>Venable didn’t tip the Sox’ ABS playbook, but he said ‘‘a mid-at-bat challenge is different than a potential strikeout or walk at-bat-ending challenge. There’s different things, different parts of the zone that we’ve talked about, different guidelines.’’</p><p>Quero said he’ll keep going with his gut.</p><p>‘‘Yeah, [based on] good feelings and . . . seeing the ball, where it’s coming from, and knowing the strike zone a little bit better,’’ he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure in Milwaukee was his first big-league action in 2½ years. He joined the Sox on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/02/19/white-sox-anthony-kay-looks-to-carry-over-success-from-japan" target="_blank" ><u>a two-year, $12 million contract</u></a> during the offseason after rejuvenating his career with a stint in Japan.</p><p>‘‘I’ve just grown so much mentally those couple of years in Japan,’’ Kay, 31, said. ‘‘That’s been a huge difference for me in my career.’’</p><p>It wasn’t pretty, but Kay turned in the best start of the Sox’ abysmal opening series, giving up two runs and three hits, striking out five and walking four in 4⅔ innings.</p><p>‘‘Definitely got a little emotional walking out to the bullpen before the game,’’ Kay said. ‘‘Definitely was a little amped up and had to hone that in a little bit. I think I did a good job of settling in after that.’’</p><p>It wasn’t exactly the season-opening sensation the Sox have gotten from a certain other Japanese veteran on their roster, but they are relying on Kay to eat up some serious innings this season while waiting for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/02/12/noah-schultz-hagen-smith-white-sox-spring-training-triple-a" target="_blank" ><u>a wave of talented arms</u></a> to emerge from Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>Kay got a preview of new teammate <b>Munetaka Murakami’s</b> prodigious power while facing him overseas.</p><p>‘‘I’m not surprised by it,’’ Kay said of Murakami’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/29/white-sox-colson-montgomery-grand-slam-murakami-homer" target="_blank" ><u>three home runs</u></a> in his first three MLB games. ‘‘I know some people are, but I’ve seen it.’’</p><h3>Numbers game</h3><p>Before Opening Day, Quero switched his jersey number from the 7 he debuted with last season to 26, which he said holds personal significance as a combination of the birthdates of his mother, his sister and his own.</p><p>It’s also the number catcher <b>Korey Lee</b> wore for the Sox until being designated for assignment at the end of spring training, ending up as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/22/white-sox-sign-catcher-reese-mcguire-leaving-korey-lee-as-odd-man-out" target="_blank" ><u>the odd man out</u></a> when general manager <b>Chris Getz</b> signed superior pitch-framer <b>Reese McGuire</b>.</p><p>Lee cleared waivers and now is wearing No. 26 at Charlotte.</p><div class="PageListL" entries.title: Michael Busch has grown into indispensable member of Cubs' lineup
entries.summary: <p>In Michael Busch’s first at-bat Monday night against the Angels at Wrigley Field, he walked on four pitches that didn’t come close to the strike zone.</p><p>After a breakout 2025 season that saw Busch finish third among first basemen in homers (34), seventh in RBI (90) and second in wRC+ (140), he has earned that respect from pitchers because they know he capitalizes on mistakes. So far this season, Busch has maintained his productive ways at the plate.</p><p>Busch isn’t the showman Pete Crow-Armstrong is, nor is he the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ clubhouse leader like Dansby Swanson or the All-Star like Alex Bregman. He’s an unassuming player who lets his game speak for itself — and it’s loud.</p><p>“He was the best first baseman in baseball last year,” Crow-Armstrong told the Sun-Times before the Cubs’ 7-2 victory. “I know you still got [Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman] and [Orioles slugger Pete Alonso]. But last year, I don’t think there was a better first baseman in baseball.”</p><p>Busch fits in with the measured and workmanlike group that team president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer has assembled. The Cubs traded left-handed pitching prospect Jackson Ferris and outfield prospect Zyhir Hope to the Dodgers for reliever Yence Almonte and Busch before the 2024 season.</p><p>At the time of the trade, Busch was the Dodgers’ No. 2 prospect, according to MLB.com, but was blocked from regular playing time because of their star-studded cast of future Hall of Famers at first and second base, and the designated hitter spot.</p><p>With regular playing time, Busch has flourished in Chicago. And now, after manager Craig Counsell said he’s going to use him more against left-handers, he’ll have even more responsibility, and Busch should fare well. He already sets the tone for the team as the leadoff hitter, even though he doesn’t fit the prototypical model of one. Crow-Armstrong said jokingly that Busch is “lacking a little bit of speed.”</p><p>“I love him in the leadoff spot,” Crow-Armstrong said. “His ability to get on base, and especially when he’s hot, makes things feel like an event.”</p><p>He’s a selective hitter with plus power and rarely chases. Crow-Armstrong lauded Busch for his work in the batting cages, saying that the first baseman works at a “very controlled level,” and that when the tempo speeds up in the game, he’s prepared for it.</p><p>“[Busch] knows what he can handle, and he does a really good job of swinging at the pitches that are right for him,” left fielder Ian Happ told the Sun-Times. “It’s not as easy as it sounds to do that. On Opening Day [Busch reached base four times and was 3-for-4 with two doubles] his ability to control the zone and get the pitches that he wanted to hit was impressive.”</p><p>Busch has room for improvement on defense. He graded out in the 36th percentile in outs above average.</p><p>“Think just being a little more efficient in all areas,” Busch said. “Especially [with] my footwork over at first, which is one thing that I want to take pride in, making sure I’m really comfortable with how I’m getting to the base, working around the base.”</p><p>But if Busch’s 2025 performance is his floor, the Cubs are in a good spot. He doesn’t garner the recognition of his teammates, but they understand Busch’s importance to the lineup.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 entries.title: Onetime Spurs guard Tre Jones talks 'Iceman' nickname and Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p>SAN ANTONIO – Tre Jones spent five-plus seasons wearing Spurs black and silver, learning the history of the organization.</p><p>The Bulls guard has also spent the last few years in Chicago, and doing so as a football fan of the Bears and quarterback Caleb Williams.</p><p>Those two worlds collided as Jones found himself stuck going between historian and politician.</p><p>There’s been a lot made of the “Iceman” nickname the last week, especially since in San Antonio there was only one “Iceman:” NBA legend George Gervin.</p><p>Williams tried to hijack the nickname and claim the legal copyright, which didn’t sit well in many circles, including with Gervin.</p><p>Jones has two horses in the race so was guarded on how he approached the entire saga.</p><p>“Yeah, the ‘Iceman,’ “ Jones said when Gervin’s name was mentioned. “George Gervin was a pioneer for basketball. Obviously, not only for (the Spurs) franchise, but the entire NBA as well. He pushed the envelope in so many ways.</p><p>“I think that as long as ‘The Iceman’ nickname isn’t disrespected and it’s kept as a sign of respect to George Gervin … you know it’s a new eras, a new generation, names can keep flying around like that.”</p><p>Plus, Jones and his Bulls teammates had a bigger nickname to worry about on Monday: “Wemby.”</p><p>Looking to avoid a winless four-game road trip, the Bulls watched current Spurs legend Victor Wembanyama put on a clinic on both ends of the floor, scoring 41 points, grabbing 16 rebounds and adding three blocks to his box score, as the home team ran away with it, 129-114.</p><p>Not that it hurt the big picture for Billy Donovan’s crew, as they dropped a half-game behind idle Milwaukee in the standings, but kept the No. 9 spot in the draft lottery odds.</p><p>And frankly after the first quarter, they were never really a threat to challenge the home team. The Bulls played San Antonio even in the first quarter 29-28, but Wembanyama and second-year guard Stephon Castle took over, combining for 23 points in the second quarter.</p><p>Not a good way to end a day that started with the news that Jaden Ivey was let go for behavior detrimental to the team.</p><p>“He’s a very talented player,” guard Josh Giddey said of the Ivey news. “Obviously the whole thing is kind of unfortunate in a way. I hope he gets the help he needs, whatever he’s going through or not going through. I do really hope he gets help. It’s not going to be with the Bulls anymore, but wherever it is I hope he gets it.”</p><p>Meanwhile, as far as the “Iceman” debate, Williams has been courtside for several Bulls games since being drafted by the Bears two years ago, and that hasn’t gone unnoticed by Bulls players. That’s why as much as Jones respects the tradition and history of San Antonio, he admittedly offered up support in what the quarterback was attempting to do.</p><p>“I like Caleb a lot,” Jones said. “He had a great year this year and the ‘Iceman’ nickname was really cool. I support that as well, but as long as there’s the respect that George Gervin deserves with it.”</p><p></p><p></p><h3>More on Jones</h3><p></p><p>Gervin wasn’t the only topic Jones had to address before the game.</p><p></p><p>Like his older brother, <b>Tyus</b>, Jones played at Duke, still bleeds blue and was horrified to watch his alma mater become the first No. 1 seed in the NCAA Tournament to lose after leading by at least 15 points at the half.</p><p></p><p>‘‘That was a tough one for sure,’’ Jones said of the game Sunday. ‘‘Last year was tough, missing free throws and the turnover at the end of the game. But this year, up 19 . . . I was back at the hotel with my family, and it was definitely tough.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I always back them. I think this is setting them up for something down the line, for sure. [Coach <b>Jon</b>] <b>Scheyer </b>has been to three straight Elite Eights now. Final Four last year. Moments away from a Final Four this year. So I think whatever is happening is just preparing them for the future, for sure.’’</p><p></p><h3>Fixer-upper</h3><p></p><p>Bulls coach <b>Billy Donovan </b>has seen a lot of positives from forward <b>Leonard Miller</b>.</p><p></p><p>The high-energy Miller joined the Bulls from the Timberwolves in the <b>Ayo Dosunmu</b> trade and has worked his way into the rotation and even some starts.</p><p></p><p>Donovan, however, wants to see him take the next step in his game.</p><p></p><p>‘‘It’s just, like, the detail of who’s he guarding? What coverage is he in? Who is in the action with him? When is he switching?’’ Donovan said. ‘‘Those are things that are happening fast where he can get caught there several times. entries.title: West Side man gunned down in West Pullman
entries.summary: <p>Nearly 90 shell casings were recovered from the scene where a man was fatally shot Monday morning in West Pullman on the Far South Side. </p><p>Jajauan Thigpen, 26, was in the street in the 800 block of West 122nd Street about 11:55 a.m. when he was shot multiple times in the body, Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Thigpen, of the city's Garfield Park neighborhood, was pronounced dead at the scene at 12:04 p.m., officials said. </p><p>About 86 shell casings were recovered from the scene, a police source said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: 2 fatally shot during fight in East Garfield Park home; 1 in custody
entries.summary: <p>Charges were pending for a man who was arrested after a man and a woman were fatally shot during a fight Monday night in an East Garfield Park home. </p><p>Two men, 44 and 31, began fighting around 9:40 p.m. at the home in the 2800 block of West Washington Boulevard when the older man pulled out a knife and attacked the younger man, Chicago police said. </p><p>But the younger man, who has a valid firearm owner identification card, pulled a gun and fired multiple shots, hitting the knife-wielding man multiple times in the body, police said. A 38-year-old woman trying to intervene was shot in the head. </p><p>Both gunshot victims were taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where they were pronounced dead, officials said. </p><p>A firearm was recovered at the scene. </p><p>The FOID card holder was in custody and charges were pending. </p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Woman leaves little to the imagination with comment to son
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife and I are disgusted by something we (and our grandson) have never before encountered. Our ex-daughter-in-law of 10 years recently told our 16-year-old grandson she kicked her latest boyfriend out because he would not have sex with her. Our grandson was very upset (as were we). Isn't this considered some sort of abuse?</p><p>Our grandson and his brother haven't lived with their mother for the last five years because they were tired of her smoking, drinking and revolving door of boyfriends. They live happily with their father and have little to do with their mother. — <i>DISGUSTED IN COLORADO</i></p><p><b>DEAR DISGUSTED:</b> Your grandson is a teenager; he isn't 8. That his mother would say what she did to him is surprising, but it wasn't "abuse." Could she have been tipsy when she said it? Fortunately, your grandson no longer lives under her roof and has a father with better judgment. Count your blessings and let this pass.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My boyfriend carries his keys and several metal accessories on a carabiner, which is always clipped to his belt loop. He lives in my home and is a frequent passenger in my car. I have noticed that his key clip and other items are damaging the paint on my car and door frames at the house as he exits and enters. I have asked him to please remove the clip or make another arrangement for his keys, and although he says he's "working on the problem," nothing changes. I'm ready to refuse entry to this key monster. Advice? — <i>DINGED IN OHIO</i></p><p><b>DEAR DINGED:</b> Only this. It seems that your irresponsible boyfriend lacks respect for other people's property or he would have dealt with this promptly. Estimate the cost of refinishing your car and door frames, and then offer him the opportunity to settle up what he owes you, or tell him it's time to move.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> One of our co-workers doesn't want to be a closer friend even though at work we say we love each other. We want to take the friendship to a deeper level, but she hesitates when we try to hang out outside of work. She has a mansion that many people in our office have seen, but she hasn't invited us over. She'll only go to the movies with us. We are worried it is because, in a movie theater, we can't talk to her. Are we getting mixed messages or coming on too strong? — <i>GIRLS AT WORK IN MICHIGAN</i></p><p><b>DEAR GIRLS:</b> You are coming on way too strong. There are work relationships and personal relationships. They are not always interchangeable. The woman may "love" working with you. But to assume that it's OK to pressure her into inviting you to her home or to be grilled about her personal life is wrong. You may mean well, but you girls need to accept the relationship as it is.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. entries.title: Popular vote plan to elect presidents is patriotic
entries.summary: <p>This year, America marks 250 years since the Declaration of Independence.</p><p>That should make us proud. It should also make us honest.</p><p>When my son was 11, we walked the Lexington battlefield in Massachusetts. As we crossed that ground, I told him our family descends from the youngest person to carry a musket there that day. He was just a boy. He stood in a different unit from his father. Father and son, both there. Father and son, both fighting for freedom. Father and son, both fighting for the right of a people to govern themselves.</p><p>Then I looked at my son and said: He was only two years older than you are now.</p><p>That moment has stayed with me. So has another truth. Our roots in the Revolution run through both Massachusetts and Virginia. We also descend from Richard Bland of Virginia, who argued for the rights of the colonies before independence was declared.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b00000" name="module-b00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>So this year, as we mark 250 years since the Declaration, we should ask a simple question: Have we finished what those brave men, women and children started?</p><p>Not yet.</p><p>We elect our mayors by popular vote. We elect our governors by popular vote. But we still do not count every vote equally when we choose our president.</p><p>Try explaining that to a child. It is awkward.</p><p>Because democracy rests on a simple idea: the person with the most votes should win. One person, one vote.</p><p>Today, that is not how presidential politics works in practice. A few swing states get most of the attention. The rest of the country is pushed aside. Millions of Americans in red states and blue states alike are told, in effect, that their votes matter less in the one race that belongs to all of us.</p><p>That is not fairness. That is neglect.</p><p>There is another way.</p><p>It is called the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nationalpopularvote.com/written-explanation" target="_blank" >National Popular Vote Interstate Compact</a>. It does not end the Electoral College. It uses it in the way the Constitution allows. The Constitution gives state legislatures the power to decide how their electoral votes are awarded. Under this plan, states agree to give their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the most votes in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. No constitutional amendment is needed.</p><p>Virginia is now close to joining. The bill has passed both houses of the General Assembly. If Gov. Abigail Spanberger signs it, Virginia would become the 19th jurisdiction in the compact, joining states such as Vermont, Delaware, Maine and Illinois. Virginia is not some side note in this story. It is one of the places where the American idea of self-government first took root. If Virginia joins now, it will not be breaking with the founding. It will be honoring it.</p><p>That is not a radical idea. It is an American one. And it should not belong to one party.</p><p>This is not about helping Republicans. It is not about helping Democrats. It is about trusting the people.</p><p>That idea is not left-wing or right-wing. It is not urban or rural. It is not Black or white.</p><p>It is patriotic.</p><p>Of course, there are still obstacles. More states would need to join. Lawmakers would need to act. Courts may weigh in. None of this is certain.</p><p>But history does not move only when success is guaranteed. It moves when people decide that something is right.</p><p>And what better time than now?</p><p>What better way to honor America’s 250th birthday than by taking one more step toward becoming the democracy we have always said we are?</p><p>The people who stood at Lexington did not risk their lives so future generations could accept minority rule. They did not fight so Americans would shrug when the person with the most votes loses.</p><p>They fought for freedom.</p><p>They fought for self-government.</p><p>They fought for the right of the people to decide their own future.</p><p>It is time to finish what they started.</p><p>Let the people decide.</p><p>Let the majority rule.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b10000" name="module-b10000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

I realized if Mozart could do this, maybe I could do that,” Smith said. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>A young boy with something to say</b></h3><p>Charles Joseph Smith was born in 1970 on Chicago's South Side. As a young child, he did not speak for several years. His worried parents took him to a series of doctors, who eventually concluded that Smith was selectively mute.</p><p>In an era when autism was understudied and widely stigmatized, it took years for the Smith family to fully understand and embrace their son’s diagnosis: autism spectrum disorder. But in that murkiness, Smith found clarity in music.</p><p>As an 8-year-old, Smith tagged along to his older brother’s piano lesson. Despite never having touched the keys, the younger Smith sibling began to play with prodigious precision. Quickly surpassing his brother, Smith grew confident in his abilities.</p><p>“I had a Mozart mentality. I realized if Mozart could do this, maybe I could do that,” said Smith, who is dressed on this day in a purple cable knit sweater, thick rim glasses, jeans and a well-worn pair of loafers.</p><p>His mother recalled how, as her son was growing up, well-meaning psychologists would tell her and her husband, a late mathematician, that their son “might be able to make some beads or something like that.”</p><p>“My husband and I were saying, we're going to all these parents meetings, counseling sessions and you mean, all that's going to happen is he is going to be making beads? We could feel that he had something more than that in him,” Emma Smith said.</p><p>“I think the music was the key to bringing him out of wherever his mind was. Temple Grandin’s 1986 memoir about living with autism and Dustin Hoffman’s 1988 performance in “Rain Man” helped him feel seen.</p><p>“I now realized people are no longer keeping it secret,” Smith said. “They just realized it's pervasive, it's everywhere. At that point, I didn't realize my gift of composing and piano was likely due to Asperger's [a form of autism].”</p><p></p><h3><b>Finding his groove</b></h3><p>As the album’s extensive liner notes point out, Smith exists somewhere between a classically trained virtuoso and an experimental outsider artist. His sound mirrors both what you may hear in storied classical music halls, but also tiny dive bars or free basement shows.</p><p>After college at Roosevelt University, Smith earned a doctorate in music from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. During his studies, he performed as a concert pianist in Italy, Germany, France and Hungary. In 2000, Smith earned an honorable mention from the French Piano Institute in Paris. But outside the structure of school, he found it hard to sustain momentum as a professional musician.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/okgalofOpPs?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Love Theme (1996)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Back home in Chicago, he found work as an accompanist for a local vocal coach at the Fine Arts Building and in South Side churches. None of it seems to go together, yet somehow it does, and it’s all the product of a singular, prolific mind.</p><p>Where “Love Theme” is a traditional classical piano piece, the punchy “Beats for Katie S.” features whistles and a spinningly fast pace. Two rare songs showcase Smith’s voice, “My Days Are Not Over For Me” and the operatic “The Five Louises.”</p><p>Smith’s giant catalog was pared down to these 10 tracks by Glenn Curran, who cofounded Sooper in 2016, alongside fellow musicians <a class="Link" href="https://vocalo.org/nnamdi-npr-music" target="_blank" ><u>Nnamdi Ogbonnaya</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://vocalo.org/sen-morimoto-diagnosis-bekoe-interview23" target="_blank" ><u>Sen Morimoto</u></a>. the tracks that really moved me and that also represented all of the different things that Charles could do, and then continued to narrow it down from there,” Curran said. “Which is kind of an But, it's also an introduction to a Chicago musician who many once assumed had little to say. </p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: HIV, AIDS infections up in Chicago after years of decline as cases rise among Latinos
entries.summary: <p>Ricardo Jiménez feels like he’s going crazy.</p><p>The leader of public health initiatives at Chicago’s Puerto Rican Cultural Center is desperately trying to find a way to keep his HIV prevention programs afloat. But amid funding cuts and a backlash against diversity and equity efforts, he worries his Humboldt Park-based health programs could be wiped out by this summer unless new funding is secured.</p><p>“People will lose their jobs and that probably will include me, too,” he said.</p><p>It couldn’t come at a more challenging time.</p><p>HIV infections are on the rise in Chicago after about two decades of decline, growing 29% between 2022 and 2024. AIDS cases are also up slightly. In 2024, there were 818 new HIV cases — and nearly half were among Latinos, the population Jiménez focuses on. That increase is particularly significant, marking the first time the racial and ethnic group accounted for most of the new diagnoses, said John Peller, CEO of the AIDS Foundation Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-120000" name="html-embed-module-120000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/28234189"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/28234189/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Chicago health officials say some early clues behind the increase among Latinos include a change in migration patterns which possibly included people who hadn’t been tested or maintained care, along with ripple effects of the COVID-19 pandemic that could have interrupted HIV care.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-c10000" name="html-embed-module-c10000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/28213472"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/28213472/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The change comes amid two contradictory trends: Testing and treatment for HIV has advanced so much that it allows people with the virus who are treated to live relatively normal lives and, critically, not transmit the virus to anyone else. But those advancements are at risk as funding for treatment and prevention for communities most at risk are under attack.</p><p>“What we’re seeing right now is really setting us back in the trajectory of the HIV epidemic and it shouldn’t be that way,” Peller said. “It’s going to ultimately cost taxpayers and society more money to take care of people who are living with HIV, who may come down with an AIDS diagnosis, [and] end up in the hospital then it would be to prevent HIV in the first place.”</p><h3>HIV cases among Latinos grow post-pandemic </h3><p>The number of Latinos living with HIV or AIDS in Chicago grew nearly 17% from 2020 to 2024 while it dropped among the white and Black population during that period, according to the most recent city data. And in 2024, there was an increase in people with a late diagnosis of HIV/AIDS — they were diagnosed with HIV and then AIDS within 12 months — and half of those 156 people were Latinos.</p><p>Chicago Department of Public Health Commissioner Dr. Olusimbo Ige said officials are looking into possible explanations, including a change in migration from 2022 to 2024.</p><p>During that time, more than 51,000 newly arrived immigrants, many who identify as Latino, resettled in Chicago. They were bused here and other Democrat-led cities by Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott as a political ploy to critique former President Joe Biden’s immigration policies. Some new cases could be among that population, which was getting tested for the first time, Ige said. People living in city-run shelters underwent medical screenings and testing.</p><p>“We want people to know that HIV is not a disease of one community or another. It is an area where we need everyone to be protected,” Ige said in an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times. “And we need to change our strategies to be community oriented and culturally appropriate, but we don’t want any community to be stigmatized.”</p><p>The increase could also be fallout of the COVID-19 pandemic. People delayed medical care because of a change to insurance or because they were afraid of falling sick with the virus, Ige said.</p><p>“Once that momentum shifts, it is hard to regain it,” Ige said. “It’s convincing people that PrEP is still important, staying connected to your care is still important, keeping your medical appointment is still important.”</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dr. Olusimbo Ige, commissioner of the Chicago Department of Public Health, says health officials are looking into what might be behind the increase in HIV cases in Chicago. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Zubaer Khan/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>PrEP is a medication that prevents HIV infection. While there is not a cure for HIV, medication, called antiretroviral therapy, can make it undetectable so an individual cannot transmit it, Peller said.</p><p>But if a person stops taking their antiviral therapy because their care is disrupted, the likelihood of transmitting HIV increases and it could result in more complex and costly treatments to get back to an undetectable viral load, Peller said.</p><p>To reach people at risk, the Puerto Rican Cultural Center went to nontraditional settings, like nightclubs and bars with special Latino music nights to offer HIV testing. It was also an avenue to inform people about medications and other resources, said Tichike Tumalan, a program coordinator. But without funding, they won’t be able to do that outreach.</p><p>“We are taking a couple steps back,” Tumalan said. “But also understanding our trans experience and also being Latino — I think we’ve always been in a position of uncertainty.”</p><p>The gap in accessing medications, in particular PreP, remains wide for Black and Latino populations, said Dr. Andrew Crone, an infectious disease specialist at Chicago-based Howard Brown Health. Cost could be one barrier, Crone said. He noted that at nearly 46% of all people living with HIV, Black patients still have the largest share of all cases and a rate disproportionate to their overall population. That rate dropped from nearly 49% in 2020 as cases dropped slightly and the number of Latino cases rose. Black residents also had the highest percentage of new AIDS cases in 2024.</p><p>There are programs that provide medication for people without health insurance or who are living in the U.S. without legal status, Crone said. Still, people are increasingly hesitant to share information with the government about their immigration or HIV status.</p><p>“We’re in a situation where people who previously knew they had access to medication and care are afraid to seek it because they are afraid of something happening to them,” Crone said.</p><p></p><h3>‘Perfect storm’ amid funding crunch </h3><p>Reaching the community most in need takes time and money. But funding for public health remains in limbo.</p><p>In February, the Trump administration announced millions of cuts to public health programs, including HIV prevention. In Illinois, the grants were restored, but funding only lasts through June, and it’s unlikely to be extended, Peller said. Those funds trickled down to the Puerto Rican Cultural Center, which is not expecting the funds to be renewed for another year.</p><p>Across the country, states facing tightened budgets are limiting access to the AIDS Drug Assistance Program, which provides HIV treatment to individuals through a combination of federal, state and local funds, according to an analysis from KFF, a nonprofit health policy research and news organization. While the program hasn’t been limited in Illinois, Peller said the AIDS Foundation Chicago, along with other advocacy groups, are pushing the state Legislature to increase funding for HIV programs.</p><p>“It’s really a perfect storm of demand and need right now for state HIV programs,” Peller said. “We are having the increasing cost from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/12/18/obamacare-aca-tax-credits-expiring-premiums-congress-january-spike-health-care-insurance" target="_blank" ><u>[Affordable Care Act] tax credits expiring</u></a>, we have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/06/medicaid-unchanged-for-now-cook-county-officials-spike-in-misinformation-and-confusion" target="_blank" ><u>Medicaid cuts</u></a> coming, and we have an increase in the number of people living with HIV in Chicago.”</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker’s office said it was monitoring legislation, but noted that any bill has to be carefully reviewed "to understand the fiscal impact," and pointed out that the Illinois Department of Public Health is developing a five-year plan to address HIV prevention and care.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d90000" name="module-d90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b><u>Where to find help</u></b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-0e5d5010-2bd9-11f1-b93e-6b53e9a7fa54"><li><b>Spanish-language resources:</b> Visit <a class="Link" href="https://hivhub.org/es/" target="_blank" ><u>https://hivhub.org/es/</u></a> for resources from the AIDS Foundation Chicago and the Center on Halsted. </li><li><b>HIV prevention services</b>: To reach the Puerto Rican Cultural Center, call (773) 278-6737. </li><li><b>Find community:</b> CALOR, 3201 W. North Ave., is hosting open houses on April 2 and and April 4 for an empowering circle for trans women, transfeminine people and those questioning. For more details visit <a class="Link" href="http://instagram.com/calorchicago" target="_blank" ><u>instagram.com/calorchicago</u></a>. </li></ul></div> </div><p>Jiménez had hoped city grants would keep their programs running. By March, the organization received another grant denial and believed they were being zeroed out of city funding. They gathered in the heart of Humboldt Park with other community groups to call on state officials to dip into emergency funds to continue HIV testing and medications.</p><p>“We are asking for entries.title: Jackson Park’s 'Gold Lady' could look like a million again, thanks to a planned restoration
entries.summary: <p>On just the right morning, when things are crisp and clear enough, the sun rises over the lake and lights up the gilded two-story Statue of the Republic in Jackson Park.</p><p>And the Gold Lady — as she's informally known — proudly faces that rising sun as she's done since 1918, draped in a tunic, crowned with a laurel and with her arms aloft. She holds an eagle-topped globe in her right hand and a staff bearing the word “Liberty” in her left.</p><p>But the spectacle, though still impressive, has been losing its luster in recent years. The gold leaf is growing dull and some of it has flaked away enough to expose the bronze underneath.</p><p>The work still shines, but not like it once did.</p><p>The Chicago Park District is now making plans to repair and regild the Gold Lady starting in May. The $1 million job includes repairing and removing the 24-foot statue's worn and flaking gold leaf and applying a new layer of the micro-thin substance over the entire work.</p><p>"It's beautiful now ... but once the gilding is on, I think people will be stunned by the transformation," Chicago Park District Director of Historic Assets Andrew Schneider said.</p><p>So here's to The Republic, for which it stands — right there at 63rd Street and Hayes Drive traffic circle. The statue was last regilded 33 years ago, so it's about time.</p><p>And it's good to see one of Jackson Park's jewels — one that lies beyond the grounds of Obamaland on the north end of the park — get some long-needed attention.</p><h3>‘Our Statue of Liberty’</h3><p>Designed by sculptor Daniel Chester French, the sculpture is a scaled-down replica of the 65-foot gilded Statue of the Republic that sat in a basin facing west toward the neo-classical Court of Honor and its high-domed Administration Building at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, held in Jackson Park.</p><p>"The 1893 World's Fair was one of the great fairs of the world," Chicago author and historian Rolf Achilles said.</p><p>"It not only brought tens of thousands of people to Chicago, but it really helped put Chicago on the map and brought people to see the new architecture in Chicago," Achilles said.</p><p>The statue was designed to celebrate the American ideals of liberty and its republic form of governance.</p><p>"That was the whole concept," Achilles said. "The sun was hitting America, and America was aglow at the time. Even if it was a white man's concept, it was still a concept and it worked, in part. And that made her a centerpiece of what people went to the fair and took home with them as visual."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Republic.</p><p>The new statue would commemorate the exposition's 25th anniversary and the century that had passed since Illinois won statehood.</p><p>The sculpture was placed on the old site of the entries.title: Three Chicago restaurants are 2026 James Beard Award finalists
entries.summary: <p>Three Chicago restaurants are finalists for this year’s prestigious James Beard Awards. And, the food industry’s highest honor announced Tuesday that the ceremony will remain in Chicago at least through 2028 — a one-year extension from what had been previously announced. </p><p>Bailey Sullivan, of West Loop’s Monteverde Restaurant & Pastificio, is a finalist in the emerging chef category. Plus, Norman Fenton of Cariño in Uptown and Jacob Potashnick of Feld in Ukrainian Village are among this year’s finalists in the best chef Great Lakes category, the James Beard Foundation announced Tuesday from The Wellsley, a private event space in Chicago’s River North, owned by the Boka Restaurant Group.</p><p>“Because it’s a time of real challenge and uncertainty, it's important to say this with certainty: Independent restaurants are not just businesses, you are the very fabric of American culture,” said Clare Reichenbach, CEO of the Beard Foundation. “You fuel economies and ecosystems. entries.title: Waves of potentially severe storms may bring 'golf ball sized hail' to Chicago area
entries.summary: <p>"Waves" of potentially severe thunderstorms are approaching the Chicago area as a moving cold front will cause temperatures to plummet more than 20 degrees Tuesday. </p><p>The storms bring a slight chance for flooding and could produce golf ball sized hail and "damaging" winds up to 60 mph in the southwest suburbs, according to the National Weather Service. A severe thunderstorm watch is in effect until 5:30 p.m. for 13 counties in Illinois including Cook, DuPage and Kane counties, the NWS said.</p><p>A ground stop was issued at O'Hare International Airport around 8:30 a.m., according to the Federal Aviation Administration. At least 10 flights were canceled and over 180 more were delayed as of 9:50 a.m., according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.flightaware.com/live/cancelled/today/KORD" target="_blank" >FlightAware. </a></p><p>Throughout the day, the Chicago area was expected to see temperatures in the high 60s to low 70s before plummeting down into the 50s by Tuesday night. </p><p>"There's just a cold front that's dropping through the area, and on the north side of that front there are much colder temperatures than there are on the south side of the front," said Rafal Ogorek, a meteorologist with the weather service. "We're currently south of the front, so that's why we're observing the warmer temperatures right now. But as the front moves through the area, those colder temperatures will move into the Chicago metro area." </p><p>A separate storm system will bring periodic rain and thunderstorms throughout the week starting Wednesday, according to Ogorek. </p><p>"That'll bring a renewed chance for showers and thunderstorms in the area." </p>

entries.title: Passover 2026 — remembering one difficult time in another difficult time
entries.summary: <p>Passover <i>and</i> April Fool's. On the same day! The possibilities are endless. I feel compelled to greet our guests at Wednesday night's Seder with a hearty, "Welcome! Let's eat!"</p><p>Not laughing? As with all jokes, it's only funny if you know the set-up: Seder means "order" in Hebrew, and the meal only comes after a protracted span of praying and storytelling. Some years we don't eat until 9 p.m.</p><p>Makes no sense, right? Then you're probably not Jewish, like 97.5% of Americans. Jews are a shrinking shard. Rather than control the world, we can't even control our own children, who wander off, as kids will.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c10000" name="module-c10000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>My wife, in her infinite wisdom, introduced a new Seder tradition: preliminary soup. We say a few throat-clearing prayers, and then her excellent, cannonball-dense, matzo ball soup is served, to fortify participants for the hour or two until the festive meal proper begins, the exact time being a tug-of-war between grey-bearded traditionalists and the younger generation, who want to eat and race back to their real lives.</p><p>I suppose the strictly religious might view early broth as the kind of canonical slippage that leads to Christmas trees and, eventually, even fewer Jews. I consider it kindness toward hungry relatives who have consented — heck, some traveled long distances — to endure this dusty rigmarole in return for a hearty meal, eventually, and all the wine they can hold.</p><p>My late colleague Roger Ebert once said that his entire political view can be summed up by "kindness." I'd like to extend that to religious orientation — if your religion doesn't prompt you to be kind, first and foremost, then it's just another tool for oppression, like the others. All religions are the same in that regard, or as I've said before: religion is a hammer: you can use it to build a house, or to hit somebody in the head. Same hammer.</p><p>Focusing on cosmetic differences seems so strange to me. "Oh, you've got an Estwing? Well, MY hammer is a Stanley. I believe the wooden handle absorbs shock better..."</p><p>Thus fortified, antisemitism rolls off me. All bigotry is ignorance married to fear. How much mental energy should be spent getting upset that the person viewing life through a keyhole caught sight of you? Someone who has lapped up the vile poison trickling through gutters for a thousand years now wants to upchuck a bit on my shoes. How hurt am I supposed to be? "Oh boo, frickin' hoo. The kneejerk hater who bought a load of idiotic bilge doesn't like me..."</p><p>Maybe I'm hardened, as a newspaper columnist who hears from haters daily. I don't want to underestimate the scary turn the country has taken after the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks, and the current war in Iran, in lockstep with our good buddy, Israel. The latest twist on antisemitism — that Israel is a monstrous evil that should have never existed in the first place and must be stamped out by force — is certainly frightening, for its popularity, though it's really just a new set of steps to a very old dance, the classic Jews Don't Belong Here Polka. Don't know the words? You can hum along: "<i>Life ... would be great ... but we've got these Jews here ... infesting ... INSERT LOCATION ... where they don't belong ... and we'd all ... be so much happier... if only they'd go live in ... INSERT SOME SPOT FAR AWAY.... " </i></p><p>See why we have a big dinner? If you had escaped arrows fired at you for the past 3,000 years, from Nebuchadnezzar to the current crop of incoming freshmen, you might be in a festive mood too. I really like Passover, and could list a dozen reasons why. Space dwindles, so I'll stick with my top four: 1) Dinner with family; 2) Special food; 3) Expressions of gratitude and 4) a great story.</p><p>Underline "gratitude." We're all slaves to something, struggling to break free. One year, I read excerpts from John Berryman's <a class="Link" href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48948/eleven-addresses-to-the-lord" target="_blank" >“Eleven Addresses to the Lord,”</a> which begins,</p><p><i>Master of beauty, craftsman of the snowflake,</i><br><i>inimitable contriver,</i><br><i>endower of Earth so gorgeous & different from the boring Moon,</i><br><i>thank you for such as it is my gift. </i></p><p>Love "boring moon." Though my favorite lines are these:</p><p><i>Fearful I peer upon the mountain path</i><br><i>where once Your shadow passed. Limner of the clouds</i><br><i>... I am afraid,</i><br><i>I never until now confessed.</i><br><i>I fell back in love with you, Father, for two reasons:</i><br><i>You were good to me, & a delicious author.</i></p><p>See why Seders take so long? Anyway, Happy Passover to those who celebrate. And to those who hate... maybe if you applied some of that incredible energy spent looking outward and condemning others to looking inward and improving yourself, well, couldn't hurt.</p>

entries.title: Bystander shot, vehicle hit by gunfire crashes on Near North Side
entries.summary: <p>Someone inside a white car opened fire at a red car, but instead hit a woman walking nearby as the attack also caused a crash on the Near North Side Monday night. </p><p>Around 9:30 p.m., someone inside a white sedan approached a red vehicle in the first block of East Chicago Avenue and began shooting, Chicago police said. </p><p>A 25-year-old woman was walking outside and was struck in the thigh by gunfire, police said. She was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where she was in fair condition. </p><p>The red vehicle was struck by gunfire and crashed into a black SUV, video shows. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>
